title: Central Ideas and Details
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Reading and Writing · Information and Ideas
summary: Find the main idea of any text, avoid too-narrow and too-broad traps, answer detail questions exactly, and read older prose and poetry with confidence.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Central Ideas and Details questions check whether you understood what a text is mainly about and what it actually says. You read one short passage (25–150 words) from literature, history/social studies, the humanities or science, and answer one four-option question. Literature passages include prose fiction, drama and poems, and some are written in older English.
The two main forms (in our own words):

items: **Main idea:** "Which choice best states the main idea of the text?" (For literature: "…the main idea of the poem" or "…what happens in the text".)
**Detail:** "According to the text, what is true about…?", "According to the text, why did the researchers…?", "Based on the text, what is [the character's] main concern?"

blocks.text: This skill belongs to the **Information and Ideas** domain, together with Command of Evidence (textual and quantitative) and Inferences. Information and Ideas is about 26% of the scored Reading and Writing questions (12–14 questions across both modules).

blocks.title: The big idea
blocks.text: The main idea is the one point that the WHOLE text supports. A detail answer must be **stated** in the text (perhaps in different words). In both cases, the right answer never goes beyond what is written.
The method for main-idea questions

items: **Find the topic:** who or what is the text about? (sea otters; Mr. Ashby; the river)

**Find the point:** what does the text say about that topic overall? Look for the turn (but, yet, however), the conclusion (thus, so, suggests that, researchers conclude) or, in fiction, the change or realisation.
**Write a one-line prediction:** topic + point. "Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating urchins."
**Test each choice with the Goldilocks check:** not too narrow (only one detail), not too broad (bigger than the text), not distorted (mixes up cause and effect, or who did what), not extreme.
**Ask: do the other sentences support it?** If most sentences in the text are examples or evidence for the choice, it is the main idea.

headers: Example (text about sea otters protecting kelp forests)
rows: covers the whole text's point, no more
By controlling sea urchins, otters help keep kelp forests healthy.
a topic much bigger than the text
Hunting has harmed many marine species along the Pacific coast.
real words from the text, wrong relationship
Kelp forests protect sea otters from hunters.
Without sea otters, all ocean life would disappear.

blocks.text: The method for detail questions

items: **Find the key word** in the question ("why… native shrubs?") and locate it in the text.
**Read that sentence and one either side.** The answer is almost always right there.
**Match meaning, not words.** The right choice usually paraphrases the text. Wrong choices often copy words from the wrong sentence.
**Do not infer.** If you have to say "probably" or "maybe", it is not a detail answer.

Reading older literary language

Some SAT literature passages come from older novels, plays and poems, often from the 1800s. The sentences can be long, the word order unusual, and some words old-fashioned. The ideas, however, are usually simple: a character who is proud, mean, kind or foolish; a speaker who is sad, grateful or thoughtful. Use these tools.

items: **Find the main subject and verb.** Long sentences are often one simple statement plus many extra phrases. Example: "Mr. Ashby, who had never in his life been contradicted by anyone of consequence, **believed** himself wise." → Mr. Ashby believed he was wise.
**Use semicolons and "yet" as signposts.** A semicolon joins two complete, related ideas; "yet" or "but" after a list of details often carries the point.
**Watch for irony.** Older narrators often praise a character in a way that actually mocks them ("his generosity extended to everything except his purse" = he is mean with money).
**Read poems by sentence, not by line.** Follow the punctuation. A sentence may run over three or four lines.

**Ask four questions about a poem:** Who is speaking? To whom or what (an "O river…" address)? About what situation? Is there a shift (But, Yet, Now)? The main idea usually sits in the shift or the last lines.
**Restore normal word order.** Poets reorder words for rhythm: "Deep in the wood a voice I heard" = I heard a voice deep in the wood.

blocks.text: **Try it.** "Ere the sun had climbed o'er yonder hill, the travellers, weary though they were, had resumed their journey." → Before the sun rose over that hill, the tired travellers had started walking again. Main idea: they were determined to keep going.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — Main idea (science)**

Sea otters are often described simply as playful animals, but ecologists regard them as essential to the health of kelp forests along the Pacific coast. Otters eat sea urchins, which feed on kelp. Where otters disappeared because of hunting, urchin numbers rose sharply and whole kelp forests were stripped bare. When otters returned to some areas, the urchins declined and the kelp grew back, along with the many fish that shelter in it.
**Question:** Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

items: A) Sea otters are among the most playful animals in the ocean.
B) Hunting has caused many marine species to disappear from the Pacific coast.
C) By controlling sea urchin numbers, sea otters help keep kelp forests healthy.
D) Many fish depend on kelp forests for shelter.

blocks.text: **Answer: C**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** Opposite focus. The text mentions this popular view only to move past it ("but ecologists regard them as essential…").
**B — ✗ Wrong.** Too broad. Only otters are said to have disappeared because of hunting; the text is about one food chain.
**C — ✓ Correct.** Topic = sea otters; point = they protect kelp by eating urchins. Every other sentence (urchins eat kelp; kelp lost without otters; kelp returns with otters) supports it. Correct.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Too narrow. A true detail from the last sentence, not the main idea.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — Main idea (prose in a nineteenth-century style)**

The following text is written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel. Mr. Ashby was a gentleman of considerable fortune and of still more considerable opinions, which he distributed among his neighbours with a liberality he never extended to his purse. He would lecture the vicar upon charity, the doctor upon physic, and the farmers upon the weather; yet when the church roof fell in, and a subscription was raised for its repair, his name was found, after much searching, at the very bottom of the list, beside the smallest sum of any.
**Question:** Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

items: A) Mr. Ashby freely gives advice to others but is unwilling to give money.
B) Mr. Ashby is the most respected and generous man in the parish.
C) The church roof fell in because Mr. Ashby refused to pay for repairs.
D) The vicar, the doctor and the farmers resent Mr. Ashby's lectures.

blocks.text: **Vocabulary help:** "physic" = medicine; "subscription" = a collection of money from many people; "liberality" = generosity.
**Answer: A**

items: **A — ✓ Correct.** Decode: "opinions… distributed with a liberality he never extended to his purse" = generous with opinions, not with money. The list of lectures + "yet" + smallest donation prove it. Correct.
**B — ✗ Wrong.** Reversed. The narrator is mocking him; the smallest donation shows he is not generous.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** Distorted cause. The roof fell in first; his small donation came afterward, when money was collected.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Unsupported. The text never tells us how the vicar, doctor or farmers feel.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — Main idea (poem in an older style)**

The following text is from a poem written in an older style. O river, thou that hast no rest, / That runn'st forever to the sea, / Thou bear'st the mountain on thy breast / In grains too small for eyes to see. / The hills that stood when time was young / Shall pass, like whispers, down thy stream; / And all the ages raised and sung / Thou carriest softly, as a dream.
**Question:** Which choice best states the main idea of the poem?

items: A) The speaker wishes to follow the river on its journey to the sea.
B) The river is a danger to the people who live in the mountains.
C) The speaker admires the river's beauty on a quiet evening.
D) Through its constant motion, the river slowly carries away even the oldest and greatest things.

blocks.text: **Four questions:** Speaker? Someone watching the river. Addressed to? The river ("O river"). Situation? The river flowing. Point? It slowly wears away everything, even mountains.
**Answer: D**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** Unsupported. The speaker talks TO the river but never wishes to travel with it.
**B — ✗ Wrong.** Off-topic. No people are mentioned, and the river works "softly", not dangerously.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** Unsupported detail. No evening is described; the poem is about time and change, not a scene.

**D — ✓ Correct.** Decode: "thou hast no rest" = you never stop; "bear'st the mountain… in grains" = you carry the mountain away as tiny bits; the ancient hills "shall pass… down thy stream." Correct.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — Detail question (social science)**

In 2019, a group of volunteers began recording the birds that visited a small public garden in their city each morning. Over three years, they recorded 64 species. Most were common city birds, but 11 were migrants that stopped in the garden only during spring and autumn, apparently to rest and feed on journeys between Europe and Africa. The volunteers now hope to persuade the city to plant more native shrubs, which provide the insects and berries that migrating birds need.
**Question:** According to the text, why do the volunteers want the city to plant more native shrubs?

items: A) To attract more common city birds to the garden
B) Because the shrubs provide food that migrating birds need
C) Because native shrubs require less water than other plants
D) To make the garden more attractive to visitors

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** Wrong group. The shrubs are linked to migrating birds, not common city birds.
**B — ✓ Correct.** The last sentence: shrubs "provide the insects and berries that migrating birds need". Insects and berries = food. A paraphrase of the text. Correct.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** Not stated. Water is never mentioned; this might be true in real life, but it is not in the text.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Not stated. Visitors are never mentioned.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Too narrow:** a true detail presented as the main idea. Ask: does the WHOLE text support it?
**Too broad:** a general statement about a bigger topic than the text discusses.
**Distorted:** real words from the passage put together in the wrong relationship (wrong cause, wrong person, wrong order).
**Opposite of the irony:** in older prose, taking the narrator's "praise" literally when it is really mockery.
**Outside knowledge:** a choice that is true in real life but not stated in the text.
**Literal reading of a poem:** choosing the surface image (a sunset, a tree) instead of what the image means (the end of life, strength).

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Before the choices, say the topic + point in one line.
Use the turn word or the last sentence; the main point is often there.
For detail questions, find the key word in the text and read one sentence before and after.
For older texts, find the main subject and verb, and translate one difficult phrase at a time.
Eliminate too narrow, too broad and extreme choices first. If two remain, pick the one that every sentence supports. Never leave a question blank: wrong answers cost nothing.

Practice
Twelve original questions in real test format, including two poems and two passages in a nineteenth-century style.

blocks.title: Central Ideas and Details — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 12 questions · untimed · one short passage per question. State the topic + point before you read the choices.

questions.p: For a long time, scientists assumed that trees growing in the same patch of forest competed fiercely for water and nutrients. Recent research has revealed a more complicated picture. Many trees are connected underground by networks of fungi, which carry sugars and nutrients from one tree to another. In some studies, large older trees appeared to pass resources to young seedlings growing in deep shade.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Older trees always grow faster than younger ones.
Fungi are harmful to most of the trees in a forest.
Seedlings grow best when they are planted in deep shade.
Research suggests that trees may share resources rather than only compete for them.
questions.e: Old view (competition) → "more complicated picture" → fungal networks pass resources between trees. D states that point. A is extreme and unsupported; B reverses the role of fungi; C distorts the last sentence.

questions.p: Rania had always thought of her grandmother's kitchen as a place of noise: pots rattling, the radio playing old songs, neighbors calling through the window. Now, sitting there alone after the funeral, she noticed things she had never seen before: the faded pencil marks on the doorframe where her own height had been measured each summer, the chipped blue cup no one else had been allowed to use. The silence, she realized, was full of her grandmother.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Rania is upset that the neighbors no longer visit the kitchen.
In the quiet after her grandmother's death, Rania finds the kitchen full of reminders of her.
Rania plans to repaint the kitchen and replace the old cups.
Rania's grandmother preferred silence to the sound of the radio.
questions.e: The passage moves from a noisy memory to a silent present filled with small signs of the grandmother, ending with "The silence… was full of her grandmother" (B). A, C and D are not supported by the text.

questions.p: In a survey of 1,200 small business owners, researchers asked what had most helped their companies survive their first five years. Access to loans and a good location were both mentioned often, but the most common answer was advice from an experienced mentor. Owners who had met with a mentor at least once a month were also more likely to report that their business had grown.
questions.q: According to the text, what was the most common answer given by the business owners in the survey?
c: Advice from an experienced mentor
Access to loans
A good location
Monthly meetings with other business owners
questions.e: The text states "the most common answer was advice from an experienced mentor" (A). Loans and location were "mentioned often" but were not the most common; D mixes up a detail about monthly mentor meetings.

questions.p:
The following text is written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel.
Miss Harriet Lane had lived forty years in the village of Ellsby and had never once been seen to hurry. She walked to church at the same pace in sunshine and in storm; she answered letters a week after they arrived, whatever their contents; and when word came that a cousin had left her a fortune, she finished her tea before she opened the lawyer's letter, remarking only that it would keep. The village, which hurried a great deal, could not decide whether to admire her or to be offended.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Miss Lane is offended that her cousin left her a fortune.
The village of Ellsby is known for its stormy weather.
Miss Lane's calm, unhurried manner never changes, and the villagers are unsure what to think of it.
Miss Lane does not care about money and refuses her cousin's fortune.
questions.e: Every detail (same pace in storms, late letters, finishing her tea before reading of a fortune) shows her unchanging calm, and the last sentence gives the village's mixed reaction: C. A and D are unsupported (she simply delays reading the letter); B turns one detail into the topic.

questions.p:
The following text is from a poem written in an older style.
I asked the oak what made it strong,
That stood unbent through winter's war;
It answered not with speech or song,
But showed the roots I had not seen before:
Deep-sunk where never wind could go,
In patient dark, through years of snow.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the poem?
c: The oak's strength comes from hidden roots that grew deep over a long time.
The speaker is afraid of the storms that come each winter.
The oak refuses to answer the speaker because it is angry.
Winter storms eventually destroy even the strongest trees.
questions.e: The speaker asks what makes the oak strong; the "answer" is its deep, unseen roots grown "in patient dark, through years of snow" (A). B is unsupported; C misreads "answered not with speech" (it answers by showing); D contradicts "stood unbent".

questions.p: Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of any warm-blooded animal relative to their size. To save energy on cold nights, many species enter a state called torpor, in which their body temperature drops sharply and their heart rate slows. In the morning, a hummingbird can take up to an hour to warm up and become active again.
questions.q: According to the text, why do many hummingbird species enter torpor?
c: To hide from predators during the night
To digest the nectar they collected during the day
To raise their body temperature before morning
To save energy during cold nights
questions.e: The text says directly: "To save energy on cold nights, many species enter… torpor" (D). A and B are never mentioned; C reverses the process (body temperature drops in torpor).

questions.p: When the novelist Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, many readers outside the Arab world discovered his work for the first time. Translations of his novels, some written decades earlier, appeared in many new languages within a few years. For a large international audience, the prize turned a writer long celebrated in Egypt into a global literary figure.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Mahfouz began writing novels only after he won the Nobel Prize.
Mahfouz was not well known in Egypt before 1988.
Winning the Nobel Prize greatly widened Mahfouz's readership beyond the Arab world.
Translating a novel is harder than writing one.
questions.e: All three sentences describe how the prize brought new international readers and translations (C). A contradicts "written decades earlier"; B contradicts "long celebrated in Egypt"; D is off-topic.

questions.p: Many people assume that the Sahara has always been a desert. Yet rock paintings in southwestern Egypt and in Libya show giraffes, cattle, and people swimming, and the beds of ancient lakes lie buried beneath the sand. Scientists now think that thousands of years ago, slow changes in Earth's orbit brought heavier rains to the region, turning much of the Sahara green for a long period.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Rock paintings are the most reliable evidence of ancient climates.
Evidence suggests that the Sahara was once much wetter and greener than it is today.
Earth's orbit changes every few years, causing sudden shifts in rainfall.
Ancient people in the Sahara were skilled swimmers.
questions.e: Old assumption → "Yet" → paintings, lake beds and the orbit explanation all show a green Sahara (B). A is extreme; C distorts "slow changes"; D is one narrow detail.

questions.p: Every Friday, Tarek's father took him to the old bookshop near Attaba Square. The owner, a thin man with ink-stained fingers, never let a customer buy a book without first asking why they wanted it. When Tarek, at ten, asked for a book about stars, the man studied him for a moment, then handed him two: the one he had asked for and a slim volume of poems about the night sky. "Facts and feelings," he said. "You will need both."
questions.q: According to the text, what did the bookshop owner always do before letting a customer buy a book?
c: He asked the customer to read the first page aloud.
He asked the customer why they wanted the book.
He offered the customer a second book about the same subject.
He checked whether the customer's parents approved of the book.
questions.e: The text states that he "never let a customer buy a book without first asking why they wanted it" (B). C happened once, to Tarek, and is not described as something he always did; A and D are not mentioned.

questions.p: In many cities, public libraries have taken on roles far beyond lending books. They offer free internet access to people who lack it at home, host job-search workshops, run homework clubs for children, and provide quiet, safe spaces open to anyone. For some residents, the library has become one of the few places where they can spend time without being expected to buy anything.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Public libraries should stop lending printed books.
Homework clubs are the most popular service that libraries offer.
Libraries now serve their communities in many ways beyond lending books.
Most city residents no longer have internet access at home.
questions.e: The first sentence states the point and the rest lists examples: C. A is unsupported; B is one example presented as the most popular; D distorts "people who lack it" into "most residents".

questions.p:
The following text is from a poem written in a nineteenth-century style.
They told me fame was like the sun,
That all the world would turn to see;
I chased it till my youth was done,
And found it would not turn to me.
But in my garden, small and plain,
The roses greet me every morn;
I count their faces, not my gain,
And bless the hour that they were born.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the poem?
c: The speaker finally becomes famous by growing roses.
The speaker regrets spending time on a garden instead of seeking fame.
The speaker warns that strong sunlight can damage a garden.
After failing to win fame, the speaker finds contentment in simple things.
questions.e: The first stanza describes chasing fame without success; "But" shifts to the small garden that the speaker now values ("bless the hour"): D. A distorts the poem; B reverses it; C takes the sun image literally.

questions.p: Engineers who design buildings for earthquake zones increasingly use base isolators: thick pads of rubber and steel placed between a building and its foundation. During an earthquake, the isolators flex, so the ground moves beneath the building while the structure above moves much less. This reduces damage not only to walls and columns but also to the equipment inside, which is one reason hospitals are among the buildings most often fitted with isolators.
questions.q: According to the text, why are hospitals among the buildings most often fitted with base isolators?
c: Isolators help protect the equipment inside a building.
Hospitals are usually built in earthquake zones.
Isolators make buildings cheaper to construct.
Hospitals are taller than most other buildings.
questions.e: The last sentence links protecting "the equipment inside" to hospitals ("which is one reason…"): A. B, C and D are never stated.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Main idea = topic + point that the WHOLE text supports.
Reject too narrow, too broad, distorted and extreme choices.
Detail answers are stated in the text, usually in different words; never infer.
Older prose: find the main subject and verb, and watch for irony.
Poems: read by sentence; ask who speaks, to whom, about what, and where the shift is.
